items.title: How Warriors GM Mike Dunleavy foreshadowed the team's quiet NBA offseason
items.content:
How Warriors GM Mike Dunleavy foreshadowed the team's quiet NBA offseason originally appeared on NBC Sports Bay Area

July is annual moving month in the NBA, 31 days of recruitment and negotiations, with many deals discussed and a few consummated. Except for the Warriors, who approached July 2026 with barely a whisper and nothing close to a roar.

It is profoundly disappointing. To their credit, though, they indicated 46 days earlier that this could be the case.

General manager Mike Dunleavy put Dub Nation on alert on May 15. Golden State’s offseason priority, he said, was to curb its maddening habit of self-destructive turnovers. To be less reckless. Smarter with the basketball.

“The top priority is to take care of the ball, limit turnovers,” Dunleavy said on the afternoon it was announced that Steve Kerr would be returning as head coach.

“And then after that, we’ll try and get better in every which way.”

As if that alone would be enough for the Warriors to make a full recovery from a 37-45 season that ended with an NBA play-in tournament dud. It was difficult to believe such a soft vision would suffice under CEO Joe Lacob, whose ambition is unlimited. Dunleavy surely was underplaying his hand. They would bait hooks, chase stars and peer under stones to improve the roster.

Wouldn’t the Warriors respond to such a disappointing season by scouring the trade market? Even if it meant parting with some future draft capital. While window-shopping around the league, however, Dunleavy & Co. quickly discovered potential trade partners were unimpressed with the available options on the roster.

The bulk of the roster consists mostly of replaceable talent. The Warriors needed a couple younger but established veterans to support the aging core. They needed, one would think, to address the acute shortage of elite athleticism.

“In the grand scheme of things, not a lot about the roster,” Dunleavy said of last season. “This just isn’t about the roster, frankly. I don’t think we came up short because of the talent on the roster. It was injuries and things we could control.”

Injuries brought an abrupt halt to the momentum generated while winning nine of 12 as the calendar flipped to 2026. Jimmy Butler III sustained a season-ending torn right ACL on Jan 19. Stephen Curry was sidelined 11 days later with runner’s knee. Moses Moody missed the final 10 games after sustaining a torn patellar tendon on March 23.

Golden State opened the 2025-26 NBA season with two elite talents, Curry and Butler, on its roster. The surrounding talent was, on its own, barely competitive. The Warriors were 12-26 – 11th in the Western Conference standings – after Butler went down. They were 9-18 without Curry and 3-7 over the final 10 games without Moody. items.title: Kentavious Caldwell-Pope signing made official, will wear No. 1 for Sixers
items.content:
SACRAMENTO, CA - FEBRUARY 4: Kentavious Caldwell-Pope #3 of the Memphis Grizzlies looks on during the game against the Sacramento Kings on February 4, 2026 at Golden 1 Center in Sacramento, California. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Rocky Widner/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images	The Philadelphia 76ers traded Johni Broome to the Los Angeles Clippers last week in order to create enough cap space under the first apron to sign Kentavious Caldwell-Pope to a veteran’s minimum deal. Yesterday, that signing was made official.

Per Sixers Public Relations:

“Philadelphia 76ers President of Basketball Operations Mike Gansey announced today that the team has signed Kentavious Caldwell-Pope. Per team policy, terms of the deal were not disclosed. 

In 51 appearances (14 starts) with Memphis last season, Caldwell-Pope averaged 8.4 points on 41.0-percent shooting (91.3% FT), 2.7 assists, and 2.5 rebounds in 21.3 minutes. He recorded a season-high 20 points on 4-of-6 shooting from beyond the arc on Jan. 2 against the Lakers.

Since entering the league in 2013, the University of Georgia product has shot at least 38.3-percent from deep in six of his 13 seasons, including a career-high 42.3-percent from three in 2022-23. 

A two-time NBA champion with the Lakers in 2020 and Nuggets in 2023, Caldwell-Pope has appeared in 67 career postseason games, averaging 9.7 points on 35.8-percent shooting from deep, 2.8 rebounds, 1.7 assists, and 1.2 steals in 32.4 minutes. 

Caldwell-Pope has appeared in 11 NBA Finals games (all starts), averaging 10.4 points, 3.1 rebounds, 1.7 assists, and 1.2 steals in 32.5 minutes. He poured in 17 points in Los Angeles’ Game 6 series-clinching win against Miami on Oct. 11, 2020. 

Originally selected by Detroit in the first round (8th overall) of the 2013 NBA Draft, Caldwell-Pope has produced career averages of 11.0 points (42.7% FG, 36.5% 3FG, 82.6% FT), 2.9 rebounds, 1.9 assists, and 1.1 steals in 963 games (784 starts) with the Detroit Pistons (2013-17), Los Angeles Lakers (2017-21), Washington Wizards (2021-22), Denver Nuggets (2022-24), Orlando Magic (2024-25), and the Memphis Grizzlies (2025-26).

Caldwell-Pope will wear No. 1 with the 76ers.“

The new piece of information was Caldwell-Pope wearing No. 1, last donned by Andre Drummond, with James Harden also being a recent Uno, and the longest-tenured Sixer to wear the number being Slammin’ Sammy Dalembert. We’ll see how much Caldwell-Pope can positively contribute coming off a couple down years in Orlando and Memphis. Undeniably, though, he has more left in the tank than a couple other veterans whom the Sixers have used to occupy end-of-roster spots in recent years. Plus, if it makes LeBron happy, we’re all happy.

items.title: USA Basketball Sending Seven First-Timers To Women's World Cup Roster
items.content:
USA Basketball finalized its 12-player roster for the FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup in Berlin, set to run Sept. 4-13, with seven players set to make their World Cup debuts. Aliyah Boston, Paige Bueckers, Caitlin Clark, Napheesa Collier, Rhyne Howard, Angel Reese and Jackie Young will all appear in the tournament for the first time, joined by veterans Kahleah Copper, Chelsea Gray, Kelsey Plum, Breanna Stewart and A'ja Wilson.

Stewart will become just the third player in national team history to appear in at least four World Cups, joining Sue Bird, who has five, and Diana Taurasi, who has four. She is the only New York Liberty player on the roster, with teammate Sabrina Ionescu notably left off.

"We'll probably have more than half of our team going to the World Cup," said Stewart, addressing the number of Liberty players expected to compete internationally.

The roster collectively holds 14 Olympic gold medals and nine World Cup titles. USA Basketball women's national team managing director Sue Bird praised the group in a statement.

"This is an incredibly talented group that has earned the opportunity to compete in Berlin," said Bird. "Wearing a USA jersey is a privilege, and I know these 12 players will embrace that responsibility as we go after another gold medal. I can't wait to see what this team accomplishes together."

Bird was named the program's first managing director last May and has overseen coaching staff and roster selections heading into the 2028 Olympic cycle, with her choices approved by the USA Basketball Board of Governors. Duke head coach Kara Lawson will lead the team, assisted by Golden State Valkyries coach Natalie Nakase, Phoenix Mercury coach Nate Tibbetts and Indiana Fever coach Stephanie White. Dallas Wings coach Jose Fernandez and Duke assistant Tia Jackson will serve as scout coaches.

Lawson addressed the difficulty of narrowing the roster to 12 players.

"It's been a long process to whittle it down to 12 players, and I think that speaks to just the talent we have in our country across the board," said Lawson. "These 12 have earned it through their play and their consistency. I couldn't be more excited about working with each of them, and I've had a good experience with each of them."

The U.S. enters the tournament as the defending champion, having won its fourth consecutive World Cup gold medal in 2022 with an 83-61 win over China in the final. 

The WNBA season will pause from Aug. 31 to Sept. 16 to accommodate the tournament, with the Liberty resuming their regular-season schedule Sept. 18 against the Minnesota Lynx. Stewart addressed the quick turnaround between competitions.

"It's really not that many days of practice," said Stewart. "Going against the best teams in the world is no joke. I think the World Cup is the harder competition between that and the Olympics just from a schedule standpoint. When we get together, we'll be ready."
